title: Yesterday I… — telling a story
title_target: Cuối tuần vừa rồi em đi Hạ Long.
goal: Tell about something in the past without sprinkling *đã* in every sentence, link events with sequence words, and use plural pronouns.
bekal: telling past events by setting the time once, at the start
linking events with *trước tiên*, *sau đó*, *rồi*, *cuối cùng*
using plural pronouns: *chúng tôi*, *chúng ta*, *bọn em*, *các anh*, *họ*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Chuyến đi Hạ Long
dialogs.intro: Monday morning on campus. Budi has just come back from his first trip outside Hà Nội, and Nam wants to hear all about it.

lines.speaker: Nam:
lines.text: Cuối tuần vừa rồi em đi đâu?
lines.id: Where did you go last weekend?
lines.literal: end week just past younger-sibling go where?
lines.baca: Kuối tuần vừa zồi em di dâu?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Em đi Hạ Long với hai người bạn ạ.
lines.id: I went to Hạ Long with two friends.
lines.literal: younger-sibling go Hạ Long with two (classifier) friend (polite).
lines.baca: Em di Hạ Long với hai người bạn ạ.

lines.speaker: Nam:
lines.id: Oh yeah? How did you get there?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bọn em đi xe khách, mất khoảng bốn tiếng.
lines.id: We took the intercity bus, about four hours.
lines.literal: group younger-sibling go vehicle guest, take about four hour.
lines.baca: Bọn em di se khák, mất khoảng bốn tiếng.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vui lắm! Trước tiên bọn em đi thuyền, sau đó tắm biển.
lines.id: So much fun! First we took a boat, then we went swimming.
lines.literal: fun very! first group younger-sibling go boat, after that bathe sea.
lines.baca: Vui lắm! Chướk tiên bọn em di thuyền, sau dó tắm biển.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hôm đầu trời mưa, nhưng hôm sau trời nắng đẹp lắm.
lines.id: It rained the first day, but the next day was really sunny.
lines.literal: day first sky rain, but day after sky sunny nice very.
lines.baca: Hôm dầu chời mưa, nyưng hôm sau chời nắng dẹp lắm.

lines.speaker: Nam:
lines.id: How many nights did you stay?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Một đêm thôi. Sáng chủ nhật bọn em về Hà Nội.
lines.id: Just one. We came back to Hà Nội on Sunday morning.
lines.literal: one night only. morning sunday group younger-sibling return Hà Nội.
lines.baca: Một dêm thôi. Sáng chủ nyật bọn em về Hà Nội.

lines.speaker: Nam:
lines.text: Hay quá! Lần sau nhớ rủ anh nhé!
lines.id: Sounds great! Next time remember to invite me!
lines.literal: interesting too-much! time after remember invite older-brother OK!
lines.baca: Hay kwá! Lần sau nyớ zủ ang nyé!

notes: ⚠️ **Notice there isn't a single *đã* in this whole story** — even though all of it is past. The time is set once in the first sentence (*cuối tuần vừa rồi*), and after that the story runs with no marker. That's how Vietnamese people tell stories, and it's beginners' number-one mistake: sprinkling *đã* in every sentence until the story sounds heavy and odd.

**Bọn em means "we" in a casual way**, used by young people talking to someone older. The standard forms are *chúng em* or *chúng tôi*. ⚠️ Keep it apart from *chúng ta*, which means "we" **including the listener**. English uses one *we* for both; Vietnamese splits them: *chúng tôi* = we (not you), *chúng ta* = we (you too).

**Vừa rồi means "just past"** and stands after its unit of time: *tuần vừa rồi* (last week), *tháng vừa rồi* (last month). Its cousin *vừa* before a verb means "just": *Tôi vừa ăn xong.* ("I've just finished eating").

**Thế à? is a sign that the listener is paying attention.** It means "oh really?" and it's practically required in Vietnamese conversation — someone who listens without chiming in at all seems uninterested. Its cousins are *Thật không?* ("really?") and *Rồi sao?* ("and then?").

**Hôm đầu and hôm sau mean "the first day" and "the next day".** *Đầu* = beginning, *sau* = after — two words you already know, paired with *hôm* (day). The same pattern works for *tuần đầu* (the first week) and *năm sau* (the next year).

**Rủ means "invite (someone along)"** and it's a warm word: *rủ anh đi* (invite me along). *Lần sau nhớ rủ anh nhé!* isn't empty politeness — in Vietnamese social life, not being invited suggests you're not that close, so this line is actually a compliment.

grammars.title: Telling a story without sprinkling đã
body: The rule fits in one sentence: **set the time once, then forget about it**. Compare the two columns — the left is correct but heavy, the right is what people actually say.

head: Too many markers
What people say
Meaning
rows: Yesterday I went to the market.
I bought vegetables, then went home.

after: ⚠️ **So when is *đã* really used?** When you want to stress that something **has already happened**, or when no time has been mentioned at all: *Tôi đã nói với anh ấy rồi.* ("I've already talked to him", so don't worry). There *đã* carries meaning; in an ordinary story sentence it just adds weight.
English marks the past on every verb — "went", "bought", "came home". Vietnamese doesn't: "yesterday" at the start does the work for the whole story, and the verbs stay exactly as they are.

grammars.title: Plural pronouns
body: Formed by putting *chúng*, *bọn* or *các* in front of the singular pronouns you've known since unit 1.
after: ⚠️ **Chúng tôi versus chúng ta is a distinction English doesn't make.** *Chúng ta đi nhé!* = "let's go!" (you're coming). *Chúng tôi đi nhé!* = "we're off!" (you're staying). English uses *we* for both and leaves the listener guessing; Vietnamese never does.
*Các* is a general plural marker that attaches to almost any word for people: *các bạn*, *các anh chị*, *các em*. To greet a group, *Chào các bạn!* or *Chào mọi người!* are both warm and safe.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Rồi* has two jobs that are easy to mix up. At the **end of a sentence** it means "already" (unit 6): *Tôi ăn rồi.* **Between two verbs** it means "then": *Tôi ăn rồi về nhà.* ("I ate, then went home"). Position makes the difference — a pattern you've seen many times in this module.

A whole story: *Sáng chủ nhật bọn em dậy sớm. **Trước tiên** đi ăn phở, **sau đó** đi chợ. **Rồi** bọn em về nhà nghỉ một chút. **Cuối cùng**, buổi chiều đi uống cà phê với bạn.* — and not a single *đã* in it.
In Vietnamese conversation, listeners are expected to make noise. Staying silent through someone's story feels cold, and these eight short words are enough to make the speaker feel heard.

blocks.title: Trời ơi — two words you'll hear every day
items: Literally "oh sky!", it's used exactly like "oh my God!" or "oh no!" — for surprise, annoyance, admiration and amusement alike. The tone of voice decides the meaning, not the words.
Its cousins: *Ôi!* (oh!, short), *Ơ!* (huh?), *Ừ nhỉ!* (oh right!). These exclamations never show up in any grammar book, but they're a big part of how Vietnamese really sounds.

exercises.prompt: Drop the unnecessary time markers. Rewrite each sentence the way people actually say it.
items: Hôm qua tôi đã đi chợ.
Tôi đã mua rau và tôi đã về nhà.
Tuần trước bọn tôi đã đi Hạ Long.
Sáng nay tôi đã dậy sớm.
Bạn tôi đã đến lúc bảy giờ.

Tối nay ____ đi xem phim nhé! (together)
____ là sinh viên Indonesia. (our group)

exercises.prompt: Put the story in order. Rewrite it numbered 1 to 5.
items: Sau đó bọn em đi chợ.
Cuối cùng, buổi chiều bọn em đi uống cà phê.
Sáng chủ nhật bọn em dậy sớm.
Rồi bọn em về nhà nghỉ một chút.
Trước tiên bọn em đi ăn phở.

exercises.prompt: Tell about your own weekend in Vietnamese. Use each linking word once.
